did_you_know.text: The chapter opens by describing a “day” appointed for the Lord: Jerusalem will be at the center of a conflict, and plunder will be distributed within it.
According to the vision, the Mount of Olives will split from east to west, and its two halves will move northward and southward, creating a very large valley.
The chapter describes a change in the pattern of light: there will be neither the usual daylight nor an ordinary night, and light will appear even in the evening.
Living waters will flow out from Jerusalem in two directions: half toward the eastern sea and half toward the western sea; their flow will continue in summer and winter.
The chapter’s vision presents the Lord’s universal kingdom: the Lord will be king over all the earth, and there will be “one” Lord, whose name will be “one.”
After the events described, Jerusalem will dwell securely, and the chapter says that there will be no more destruction in it.
The nations that remain will go up to Jerusalem every year to bow down to the King, the Lord of Hosts, and to celebrate the Feast of Tabernacles.
Any of the families of the earth that do not go up to Jerusalem to bow down to the Lord will receive no rain, according to the chapter’s description.

Holiness will appear even on the bells of the horses, and the pots in the Lord’s house will be like the basins before the altar; in this way, the chapter describes holiness extending even to everyday vessels.
At the end of the chapter, it says that every pot in Jerusalem and Judah will be holy to the Lord, and there will no longer be a “Canaanite” in the house of the Lord of Hosts.
